title: Trump's economic strategy resemble similar policies in East Asia
description: Much of the Trump administration's economic policy has been inspired by successful industrial policies successful in East Asia, including those
body:
Much of the Trump administration's economic policy has been inspired by successful industrial policies successful in East Asia, including those of competitor, China. Will those policies work in the U.S.?   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    JOEL ROSE, HOST:  Did you catch what Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a speech at the Acropolis in Greece this week? It was striking.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)MARCO RUBIO: We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power, to take back control of our critical supply chains, to reindustrialize our economy.ROSE: Basically, industrial advancement, Rubio argues, is a national security goal. The Trump administration has been intervening in private businesses, using government funds to invest in key sectors and even taking out direct stakes in companies. NPR's Emily Feng reports that this model draws on industrial success stories in Asia.EMILY FENG, BYLINE: Back in 2018, during his first term in office, President Trump started making the case for more U.S. government intervention in sectors like steel to spark technological and manufacturing growth.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: You need some help from the government to get it started in the right direction.FENG: And in his second term, his administration has moved beyond just tax breaks and tariffs. It's begun programs inspired by state venture capital funds. They seed semiconductor and rare earths and AI work abroad. This year, the government has invested directly in critical minerals companies. It's now even taking a portion of revenue from semiconductor companies Nvidia and AMD, something Trump says the U.S. deserves to do.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)TRUMP: I said, so if we're making it possible to build, we should get a percentage of the things that are taken out.FENG: Post World War II, industrial policy like this was highly associated with governments with more centralized economic planning, but it actually has American roots.JOEL DODGE: Industrial policy, in many accounts, got its start with Alexander Hamilton and his report on manufacturers.FENG: Says Joel Dodge, director of industrial policy and economic security at Vanderbilt University. Though he notes industrial policy really took off in East Asia in the 20th century.DODGE: China, Taiwan, South Korea, use the tools of industrial policy - whether that's subsidies or state-run investment banks or geographic clusters and place-based policy - to tremendous effect.FENG: And now industrial policy has fully boomeranged back to the U.S. That's evident in the work Mike Schmidt did. He used to direct the CHIPS program, a $39 billion initiative at the Department of Commerce which began under the Biden administration.MIKE SCHMIDT: It was about onshoring, semiconductor manufacturing, to the United States.FENG: That happened, and the initiative is still ongoing under the Trump administration. Schmidt says he witnessed a shift in the conversation across the U.S. government starting in Trump's first term.SCHMIDT: I think what changed was the perceptions of our relationship with China.FENG: And global supply chains with China, which before had made goods cheaper and faster to make...SCHMIDT: Those same supply chains suddenly look very different if that integration is with an adversary or competitor.FENG: Ironically, China is one of the most prolific and successful cases in using industrial policy. Brad Parks at William & Mary in Virginia has spent years studying how China subsidizes key companies and industries at home and abroad. And since last year, he's noticed a striking similarity between U.S. industrial policy and that of China.BRAD PARKS: I think what the Trump administration effectively did was they said, there's certain aspects of what Beijing is doing that are attractive to us, and we don't need to reinvent the wheel.FENG: Particularly when it comes to energy and natural resources.PARKS: Taking equity stakes in critical mineral assets overseas is like taking a page right out of Beijing's playbook.FENG: The Trump administration has taken industrial policy one step farther than China, however, by having the state directly hold equity in critical mineral companies.PARKS: Whereas, you know, in China, it's usually state-owned companies that are taking these ownership stakes.FENG: And some U.S. deals have involved firms and funds with personal connections to the administration.DODGE: One of the notable developments under the second Trump administration in particular, which is how unilateral and personalist industrial policy has become.FENG: That's Dodge at Vanderbilt again, arguing that approach opens up the U.S. to the risk of corruption. Rubio's speech in Greece, however, made the case the U.S. has no time to lose.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)RUBIO: We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all.FENG: And Rubio framed industrial policy in militant terms, as a fight for, quote, "dominance of the technologies and industries of the future." Emily Feng, NPR News, Washington.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

title: Week in Politics: Hegseth's livestream backlash; Greece ambassador Guilfoyle scandal
description: Week in Politics: Hegseth's livestream backlash; Greece ambassador Guilfoyle scandal
body:
Week in Politics: Hegseth's livestream backlash; Greece ambassador Guilfoyle scandal
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-5995114/nx-s1-9959897" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      Bipartisan blowback on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's plans to livestream a military execution, plus a scandal involving Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US Ambassador to Greece.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT SIMON, HOST:  There has been pointed and bipartisan objection to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's plan to livestream a military execution. The Pentagon announced this week that Nidal Hasan will face a firing squad in December. He is the former Fort Hood Army psychiatrist who fatally shot 13 people and wounded nearly three dozen others in 2009. NPR senior contributor Ron Elving joins us. Ron, thanks so much for being with us.RON ELVING, BYLINE: Good to be with you, Scott.SIMON: Secretary Hegseth told Real America's Voice that, quote, "it's public because people need to understand that there are serious consequences for these types of things." But many in his own Republican Party disagree, aren't they?ELVING: They say it's a bad idea - beyond disgusting, in the words of Thom Tillis of North Carolina, a Republican senator, whose vote enabled Hegseth's confirmation last year. They're saying it's medieval, even barbaric, comparing it to public executions by ISIS and other terrorists or radical regimes such as the Taliban and Afghanistan.But let's be clear - the issue now after all these years is not crime and punishment. The 2009 crime is beyond dispute, and even those with the deepest doubts about the death penalty itself see its rationale and its application in this case. The dispute now is over making a spectacle of it. No U.S. serviceman has been put to death since 1961, back before the Vietnam escalation. And no American has been executed publicly since 1936 - nine decades ago.Hegseth says the livestream will send a signal that there are consequences, but does anyone think someone who did what Nidal Hasan did thought his actions wouldn't have consequences? This is tantamount to saying global terrorists need to be reminded that suicide bombing has downside risks. Trump was asked about this spectacle, said he gave it the green light, absolutely. But Vice President JD Vance said yesterday there were weeks ago before the December 3 date, and things could change.SIMON: Also this week, The Wall Street Journal reported that the U.S. ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, asked a Trump donor to send her $100,000 to cover credit card debt just before her confirmation hearings last year, and to do it secretly. Is the ambassador's goose cooked?ELVING: Well, the water's certainly hot enough. It depends on the call of the chef as to whether it's become too hot. The president said it was too bad but said little else. And the unseemly request for 100,000 and the access to the Trumps that was at issue will add further to the narrative of corruption surrounding the Oval Office and the first family in general in this second term.Guilfoyle first came in contact with the Trump operation as a news personality on television. She was considered a catch because 20 years ago, she had been married to California's Democratic governor, Gavin Newsom, a Democrat. And she later became engaged to Donald Trump Jr. during his father's first term and was seen with him at the party's 2024 convention, but that relationship ended later that year. Trump Jr. has subsequently married someone else.The main issue of this midterm election, Scott, as we know, is affordability. The issue of government corruption and abuse of public trust, though, is rising fast. And if voters come to link what they don't like in the economy with what they don't like to hear about administration figures selling access, that would add more jet fuel to the anti-incumbent flames.SIMON: Some serious debates this week in battleground states for the midterms - Maine, Michigan, Georgia and Iowa. What stood out to you?ELVING: The common theme was the struggle Republican nominees were in with Trump's tariffs and Trump's war with Iran. They were hamstrung by their need to show independence from those policies, even as they maintained support for the president and the party. At this point, it's clear that Republicans are hoping the Democrats have peaked and the numbers will balance out again. But Republicans are also fearful that the Democrats have not yet peaked and the next round of polls will find them pulling away toward big gains in the House and perhaps a new majority in the Senate.SIMON: NPR's Ron Elving. Thanks so much.ELVING: Thank you, Scott.

body:
U.S. imposes sweeping sanctions on International Criminal Court   The U.S. has announced sanctions against the International Criminal Court, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio vowing to dismantle the world's only permanent war crimes tribunal.

    
        Politics
    


                  
            October 10, 20267:40 AM ET
         
      

      
      U.S. imposes sweeping sanctions on International Criminal Court
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-5996606/nx-s1-9959707" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    




      The U.S. has announced sanctions against the International Criminal Court, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio vowing to dismantle the world's only permanent war crimes tribunal.   


    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT SIMON, HOST:  This year's Nobel Peace Prize was meant to bolster international humanitarian law and went to a South African jurist who has worked on the International Criminal Court, among other places. But the Trump administration wants to dismantle that court and accuses it of trying to prosecute Americans. NPR's Michele Kelemen reports on new U.S. sanctions against the world's only standing war crimes tribunal.MICHELE KELEMEN, BYLINE: Secretary of State Marco Rubio calls the ICC a rogue court and says the U.S. is now cutting off its resources and crippling its ability to operate.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)MARCO RUBIO: America never joined the court. We don't need that court, and we don't want it.KELEMEN: In a video message, Rubio accused globalist experts - as he called them - of wanting the ICC to go after Americans.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)RUBIO: They want the International Criminal Court to do more, including the prosecution of American citizens and service members that are defending their country. They want to prosecute Border Patrol agents that are protecting our nation's borders, and they want to prosecute our elected leaders.KELEMEN: But U.S. personnel are not the subject of any current investigation. The ICC suspended its look into the U.S. role in Afghanistan, even as it continues to prosecute crimes by the Taliban there. The Trump administration has criticized another big case - the arrest warrant against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over Gaza. This year's Nobel Peace Prize winner, Navi Pillay, says international law and human rights are under threat. She spoke in Nuremberg, site of the first major international war crimes tribunal against the Nazis.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)NAVI PILLAY: These efforts that we are now seeing, which are attempts to weaken international criminal justice, endanger the progress painstakingly made since Nuremberg.KELEMEN: The president of the International Criminal Court rejected the U.S. sanction, saying the court will not be deterred. The U.S. is giving companies six months to wind down their ties to the court. Indiana University professor David Bosco, who's written a book about the ICC, says this was meant to be a centralized place for war crimes victims to seek justice, instead of having courts for each and every conflict.DAVID BOSCO: That was the - what happened during the 1990s, of course, was they set up, you know, a special court for the Balkans. They set up a special court for Rwanda. And I don't think it makes sense to anybody to do that rather than having a centralized court. The key question is - how broad is the jurisdiction of that court going to be?KELEMEN: The court only has jurisdiction in member states, and that does not include the U.S. Secretary Rubio says he expects U.S. allies who rely on the U.S. military for their defense to, quote, "rein in" the court.Michele Kelemen, NPR News, Washington.

title: Politics chat: Trump announces fuel deal with Russia. What does it mean for sanctions?
description: Politics chat: Trump announces fuel deal with Russia. What does it mean for sanctions?
body:
Politics chat: Trump announces fuel deal with Russia. What does it mean for sanctions?
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-5996550/nx-s1-9960474" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      President Trump announced a deal to import Russian fuel to the U.S. We look at what this means for the sanctions he recently signed off on against Russia, as well as the U.S.'s support for Ukraine.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:  President Trump on Friday said he has an agreement to import millions of tons of diesel from Russia. The idea is to lower prices at the pump for Americans, but analysts say the amount that would be released from Russia won't really make a difference in the U.S. market. So who is this deal really helping? We're joined now by senior national political correspondent Mara Liasson. Good morning, Mara.MARA LIASSON, BYLINE: Good morning.RASCOE: The president pretty recently signed in new sanctions against Russia. There's a 2022 law against importing any oil or petroleum products until Russia ends its war against Ukraine. So what is the president doing?LIASSON: Well, one thing he's doing is struggling, without much success, to bring down diesel and gas prices. He's tried a lot of things. The latest now is removing sanctions on Russia, even though, as you just said, that might not make much of a difference in prices. Then the sanctions that Trump signed off on less than a month ago targeting Russia's energy revenues, which helped Russia fund its war against Ukraine - now the U.S. is going to be adding to those revenues. And Congress, with big bipartisan support, passed a law just a couple of days before that giving Trump expanded tariff powers specifically in hopes he would use them to put more economic pressure on Russia. Now he seems to be doing exactly the opposite thing.And then yesterday he went even further against Ukraine, saying that its leader, President Zelenskyy, should be replaced with someone more willing to make a deal with Russia. He has asked Ukraine to stop bombing Russian oil refineries. He has not applied similar pressure to Russia to stop bombing Ukrainian energy grid assets or civilian targets. He has blamed the bombing of Russian oil refineries by Ukraine on high gas prices, even though it's the Iranian war that has had a major impact on prices.RASCOE: Well - and speaking of Iran, isn't Russia helping Iran in the war?LIASSON: That's right. According to U.S. intelligence, Russia is providing real-time tracking data to Iran, which helps them strike U.S. targets in the Middle East. So the lifting of these Russian oil sanctions - Trump is helping an important ally of Iran's.RASCOE: The Pentagon said last week they'd be livestreaming the execution of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist who, in 2009, killed 13 people and wounded 32 at Fort Hood, Texas. Vice President Vance seemed to walk that back on Friday. What can you tell us about that?LIASSON: Well, the execution is supposed to be livestreamed, according to the Pentagon. There hasn't been a public execution in the U.S. since 1936. There hasn't been a military execution since 1961. So this is a remarkable decision. And public executions like this happen in places like Iran or Afghanistan or Somalia, Saudi Arabia, North Korea, not in the Western world. And this is something that makes even the vice president of the United States a little squeamish. JD Vance said he defended the execution of Hasan - who, by the way, is in a wheelchair - but he said he wouldn't be watching. And President Trump was also asked if he was going to watch it, but he didn't answer.RASCOE: You've been watching - switching gears here, you've been watching campaign ads, which are really saturating markets in states like Texas and Ohio. When it comes right down to it, do we know if people vote based on ads or, especially at this point, based on their pocketbooks?LIASSON: Well, if polls are accurate, they're voting their pocketbooks because Republicans have had a tremendous financial advantage to run as many ads as they want to on social media. They're only limited by 24 hours in a day in terms of buying ads on television. But those ads do not seem to be changing the dynamic of these races, which are leaning towards Democrats in many places where Trump won by double digits in 2024.People are just sour on the economy. They feel that their pocketbooks are being squeezed. They can't afford the things they used to be able to afford. And even though in the past, the vast majority of races where one candidate spends more, that candidate tends to win, we're going to find out in November how important money is in this election.RASCOE: That's NPR's Mara Liasson. Thank you so much.LIASSON: You're welcome.

title: Reshaped civil rights mission at Justice Department transforms its work, workforce
body:
Harmeet Dhillon, assistant attorney general for civil rights at the Department of Justice, during an interview in Washington, D.C., in August 2026.
                
                    Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images
    

   
   When Harmeet Dhillon took over as the new chief of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division last April, the conservative attorney vowed to radically reshape the storied unit and its mission.   Over the past 18 months, Dhillon has moved aggressively to make that goal a reality. She has pushed out hundreds of longtime attorneys, replaced many of them with inexperienced ideological allies, and used the division's enforcement powers to pursue President Trump's MAGA agenda, according to four current and former division officials.   Three of the individuals spoke on condition of anonymity out of fear of retribution.   
   At the root of these changes is Dhillon's vision of the Civil Rights Division and its mission that dramatically departs from tradition.   Created almost 70 years ago during the movement to end racial segregation, the Civil Rights Division historically has sought to combat discrimination and protect the constitutional rights of all Americans in everything from voting and housing to employment, education and policing. The division's priorities have shifted from administration to administration, although its core work has remained consistent.   
   But Dhillon, who was born in India and immigrated to the U.S. as a child, argues that over the years the division's mission has narrowed to protecting the rights of just one segment of society: people of color.   In her view, that has created a form of "benevolent racism" designed to punish "the descendants of those who may have been responsible for the sins of the past."   "As the logic goes, the white oppressors of years past kept Brown and Black people down, why not give them a taste of their own medicine?" she said last November at an event for the conservative Federalist Society. "That's the thinking really that underlies a lot of our civil rights enforcement work."   Transformed focus since Trump took over   That all changed, she said, in 2025 when President Trump returned to office and Dhillon arrived at the Justice Department.   
   Since then, the division has dropped investigations and withdrawn statements of interest in dozens of cases, including those involving voting rights, racial discrimination and civil actions against anti-abortion activists.   
   It has ended investigations into police departments over alleged constitutional violations.   Some of the most aggressive work of her tenure has been on the voting front, where the division has sent monitors to keep tabs on states' primary elections, and filed lawsuits demanding voter information from a slew of states, in furtherance of Trump's focus on alleged election fraud by noncitizens.   State election officials — Republican and Democratic — have pushed back, accusing the Justice Department of overreach. Judges have tossed more than two dozen of the department's lawsuits, including most recently in Georgia.   
   Education has been another active front.    In just the past two months, the Civil Rights Division has accused law schools at the University of California, Berkeley and Duke University as well as the medical schools at the University of California, San Francisco and George Washington University of discriminating against white and Asian students in admissions.   It also has sued UCLA and Harvard for allegedly allowing antisemitism to flourish on campus.    In August, a federal judge dismissed the department's lawsuit against Harvard, finding the claims of antisemitism were "too isolated and episodic" to prove the school was violating civil rights laws.    In a statement to NPR, Dhillon defended the division's work under her leadership.   "Under this administration, the division has held universities accountable for antisemitic harassment, defended the constitutional rights of Americans of every faith, and protected the integrity of federal elections," she said. "Civil rights laws exist to protect individuals from discrimination, and that is exactly how we enforce them. Critics calling equal enforcement 'weaponization' are telling on themselves."   
   While several sections have seen drastic changes in their work, not every unit has been affected to the same degree, three current and former division officials say.   Sections that address housing and disability rights, for example, are still doing a lot of the work they've traditionally done. Last year, for example, the department sued Uber for denying rides to passengers with service dogs or wheelchairs.   Out with the old, in with the new   One of the ways Dhillon has moved to implement her vision is through changes to those who do the work: the division's lawyers and staff.   
   Early on in her tenure, she accused division attorneys of pursuing a left-wing agenda.   "The job here is to enforce the federal civil rights laws, not woke ideology," Dhillon told Glenn Beck in an interview last year. She encouraged attorneys and staff who didn't want to implement her vision of the division's mission to leave the department.   Up to 80% of the division staff did exactly that in a wave of departures that has decimated the division's institutional knowledge.   
   Much of the mass exodus occurred during the height of the Trump administration's Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE cuts, and current and former division officials say many people left or opted to retire early to prevent staff cuts imposed from on high.   Current and former officials say that has left the division shorthanded — depleted of talent, expertise and basic manpower.   "There are so few people there doing civil rights work at all," said Georgetown Law professor Christy Lopez, who worked for more than a decade in the division before leaving in 2017.   Since Trump returned to office, some 300 attorneys have left the division, according to current and former officials. The Justice Department says some 130 have been hired to replace them.    There are now more division attorneys hired during the second Trump administration than there are holdovers from previous administrations, according to current and former officials.   
   Accusations of political hiring   Current and former officials say Dhillon has changed the hiring process, shrugging off rules that were meant to insulate it from partisan political considerations.   The rules were put in place some two decades ago after a scandal over political hiring during the George W. Bush administration, when the division lost some 70% of its attorneys and political appointees were accused of prohibiting attorneys from investigating cases.   In response, the division changed its policies to give non-political career staff a leading role in hiring. Career attorneys would review resumes, conduct interviews and then write a memo recommending a candidate to hire. The division's front office would then review the memo, and send it to the attorney general for a final decision.   
   The recommendation was almost always honored, current and former officials say.   
   "Those rules were put in place to prevent politics from dictating who gets a job with the Civil Rights Division rather than merit, rather than their experience and their skills and their commitment to civil rights work," Lopez said.   Under Dhillon, however, the front office, which is made up of political appointees and ideological allies, has removed the usual career staff from the process and taken the lead in hiring.   A Justice Department spokesperson denied that any changes have been made to the hiring process.   "Career staff hire career staff, just as in prior administrations. Any claim otherwise is a deliberate misrepresentation driven by political bias," the spokesperson said. "The result is 130 outstanding new attorneys, many of whom clerked for federal district and appellate judges. We are proud of every one of them, and they are already strengthening the Division's enforcement work."   
   But current and former officials say political ideology appears to be a significant factor in hiring decisions. Some of the new hires have previously worked for conservative legal groups, including the Pacific Legal Foundation and Only Citizens Vote Coalition.   There also are serious concerns about the qualifications of many of the people being hired.   Current and former officials say most of the attorneys who have been hired don't have much experience — if any — in civil rights work. Some of them have little legal experience at all, which has hampered some of the division's efforts to pursue Trump's agenda.    "I could understand it if Harmeet wanted to bring in people who could both further the president's priorities and also continue with the division's enforcement work, its traditional enforcement work," said Dena Robinson, who left the division last year and now works at the ACLU. "But that's just not happening anymore."

title: In one of the country's most competitive districts, a Democrat tries to keep her seat
description: In this file photo, Rep. Marie Gluesenka
body:
In this file photo, Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) listens at a House Appropriations Committee hearing on July 14, 2026 in Washington, DC. Gluesenkamp Perez is seeking reelection in one of the most competitive seats in the country.
                
                    Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
    

   
   The fight for which party will control Congress is zoning in on one competitive district in southwest Washington state.   The 3rd Congressional District is a mix of urban, industrial and rural communities with inland and coastal areas. It prides itself on its political independence. President Trump won this congressional district three times. But Democratic Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez flipped the district blue in 2022. Now, the Republican nominee, state Sen. John Braun, believes he has a shot at winning it back.   "A lot of districts these days are pretty predictable in terms of their politics," Braun told NPR during an interview at his small manufacturing business. "The third is not. You got to go earn those votes."   
   The competitive race has a lot on the line, most notably potential control of the House. Democrats likely need Gluesenkamp Perez to hold this seat if they want the House majority. Republicans need Braun to win if they want to keep power and help shepherd Trump's agenda across the finish line before his presidency ends.   Both are at somewhat of a disadvantage. Gluesenkamp Perez is the incumbent in an election cycle that is experiencing an anti-incumbency wave. For Trump-endorsed Braun, the midterm elections tend to be a referendum against the party in power and Republicans have an unpopular president in charge.   The biggest struggle, though, will be appealing to the various communities throughout the district. Urban Vancouver, the district's most populated city, has different needs than the rural coastal towns along the Pacific Ocean.   "They want you and expect you to show up and represent their interests," Braun said. "It gives you a little bit of freedom to vote more independently. But you also have to show up and explain your vote."   Walking the party line    The candidates are really not that different.   Both Gluesenkamp Perez and Braun are considered moderates within their parties, both own small businesses and both reside in rural towns. Both are centering front-of-mind issues for voters in the area. That includes bolstering blue collar work in manufacturing, natural resources, and supporting small businesses. Where they diverge is on some of the traditional partisan faultline issues such as abortion.   
   There is a balancing act each candidate must perform because partisan politics don't land well in Washington's 3rd District.   This has long been one of the most competitive seats in Congress — former Republican Rep. Jaime Herrera Beutler often faced fierce races to keep her seat. She was ousted in the 2022 primary after voting for Trump's impeachment following the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol.   "We don't vote down the ballot one way or the other. Trump can win the city, but Marie Gluesenkamp Perez can win the city as well on the same ballot. So it's really person specific," Longview, Wash., Mayor Erik Halvorson told NPR.   "I think loyalty matters, especially for an incumbent," Halvorson said. "I think that polished candidates are not a necessary requirement for Longview and Cowlitz County. I think you just have to be authentic."   When a candidate can't rely on the partisan label next to their name on the ballot, they have to lean on other strengths. Halvorson stressed the need to understand local issues.   Longview used to be solely known for the timber industry. It was founded to house employees of the local timber mill. But as the natural resource economy changed and the logging industry shrank, mills closed and jobs vanished.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                In this file photo, a logging truck drives on the Interstate 5 bridge that spans the Columbia River and connects Portland, Ore., with southwest Washington state, part of the 3rd Congressional District, on Feb. 13, 2024.
                
                    Jenny Kane/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jenny Kane/AP
    

   
   "I do feel like the tariffs have hit a lot of our industry here hard on the federal level," said Halvorson.   That's where John Braun feels he has a distinct advantage in this race. He owns Braun Northwest Inc., an emergency vehicle manufacturing facility. Walking through his manufacturing facility, Braun pointed out all the different materials used to build an ambulance or fire truck. The cost of those materials has increased because of tariffs and the price hike is passed onto consumers, which in Braun's case, mostly consists of American cities and municipalities.   
   Braun thinks that makes him uniquely qualified to advocate for the trades and did so regularly during his time in the state legislature. While Braun has Trump's endorsement, he hasn't pegged himself as a loyalist. One issue he would break with Trump on, Braun said, is tariffs.   "There are some appropriate uses for tariffs. But kind of the indiscriminate use, the broad use, the blanketed use, just that doesn't work," he said. "We need to be a little more thoughtful on tariff policy."   Gluesenkamp Perez backlash   Vancouver, Wash., is the urban center of this congressional district and the city has recently come into its own.   Considered to be part of the Portland, Ore., metro area, many Vancouverites argue their city's identity is unique. Gretchen Hoyt's family has lived here for four generations. She was always slightly resentful of outsiders (and insiders) smooshing the two towns into one.   
   Vancouver has put a lot of money into development. They have repurposed historic buildings into multiuse spaces and made the downtown more walkable. The city built a waterfront along the Columbia River that houses luxury apartments and classy eateries – the kind of restaurants Hoyt notes are "special occasion meals" because they're too pricey for the locals to eat at frequently.    She admits all the updates have beautified her hometown and inspired residents to spend more of their time and money in Vancouver. The investment has also led to growth and Hoyt worries a place that used to be a reprieve from high Portland housing prices has developed a similar reputation for being unaffordable.   "It's so hard to buy a house here right now," she said. "It's like everything .. is over $700,000 and for things that are just aren't worth that."   Another thing that has changed about Vancouver is its politics.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                In this file photo, a voter drops his ballot in a ballot drop box in Vancouver, Wash., on Nov. 5, 2024.
                
                    Amanda Loman/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Amanda Loman/AP
    

   
   Clark County, where Vancouver is located, has slowly gotten bluer since 2008. Vancouver itself, Hoyt observed, has shifted toward the progressive side of the scale. That progressive tilt proposes trouble for Gluesenkamp Perez, especially since Clark County is one of two counties she consistently won since her first run for Congress.   
   Two congressional votes that have ruffled feathers among Clark County Democrats. Gluesenkamp Perez voted in favor of a Republican sponsored bill dubbed "The Don't Say Trans Bill," which would require parental consent if a public school student wanted to go by a different name or gender in the classroom.   She also voted for the SAVE Act, claiming the controversial Republican-led voter I.D. legislation spawned by Trump would help secure America's election system.   
   "People feel betrayed because people thought, 'OK cool. She owns her own business. … Really. Like I'm one of you.' Then it felt like that was just a schtick in order to get the blue vote," Hoyt explained.   Gluesenkamp Perez defended her approval of the legislation.   "I do not support noncitizens voting in American elections — and that's common sense to folks in Southwest Washington. Voting in our nation's elections is a sacred right belonging only to American citizens, and my vote for the SAVE Act reflects that principle," she wrote in an April statement.   Gluesenkamp Perez did not respond to NPR's multiple interview requests.   In retaliation for those votes, progressive Democrats in Vancouver put up a primary challenger on Gluesenkamp Perez's left. While the congresswoman ultimately won one of the top two general election seats in Washington's open primary system, it exposed her vulnerability among the district's Democratic base.   "Nobody is happy with Marie, but they're not voting for John. So they're voting their conscience. It feels like the lesser of two evils," Hoyt said.   Beyond the cities    The impact of tariffs, regulation — and the national economy as a whole –- has the ability to make or break rural communities across the district. Any changes are acutely felt in the coastal region.   Kathleen Nisbet, owner of Goose Point Oysters, took over her family's shellfish farm in Bay Center, Wash., a small town of about 200 people next to the Pacific Ocean.   
   Nisbet has lived in the remote Pacific County town pretty much her whole life. She has seen a once prosperous area, which was propped up by aquaculture industries, transition into somewhat of a ghost town.   To her, the vacated businesses are a testament to how regulations have suffocated small shellfish farms. Nisbet counted on her fingers ten different regulatory agencies she must pay and answer to in order to keep her doors open and estimated she spends around $200,000 a year on agency fees.   "The regulations that we have been dealing with for the last 25 years have impacted our areas in that we've lost our farmers and we've lost our fishermen," Nisbet said.   Nisbet isn't against regulation. Her qualms are they aren't streamlined, they change frequently and are cost prohibitive for small and medium sized producers.   Now, Nisbet is dealing with another problem: Trump's trade war.   "We've lost over 50% of our international sales due to the current political climate between us and Asian countries," she said.   
   The concern is, if the trade wars continue or worsen, that there will be an even steeper decline to the industry area was built on. More farms will close or consolidate with big fisheries. The identity of the area could disappear.   "We need to make sure that we are building community resilience through natural resources, which has been the traditional backbone of our communities," she emphasized.   Nearby Ilwaco has also been on the receiving end of the industrial downfall. While there is some semblance of natural resource extraction, such as timber, seafood catches and cranberries, for the most part, the coastal town of about 1,400 people has had to pivot to invigorate the economy.   The number one industry in Ilwaco is now hospitality. Restaurants, motels and small shops welcome visitors to the town, a significant portion of whom travel through on their way to or from Cape Disappointment State Park. The town has been working to open more businesses that would attract visitors. Most recently, Ilwaco Cider Company, the town's only brewery, opened its doors.   
   Ilwaco councilman Matt Lessnau, who grew up in the town and moved back during the pandemic, said the cidery is the perfect example of what Ilwaco is trying to build.   "It really has been a tremendous asset in really growing the kind of businesses that we want to see grow in Ilwaco," he said.   
   But there is a limited tourism season. The town makes the majority of its revenue during the summer months and it relies on federal dollars to help with infrastructure needs because the local tax base isn't there — only about half the population lives in the town full time.   The rural parts of Washington's 3rd District may have fewer people but it's still influential. Pacific County voted for Trump in 2024 but also elected Gluesenkamp Perez. She narrowly won this county in 2022, too.   Lessnau said a congressional candidate needs to understand the local issues of the rural coastal towns to be electable. Additionally, he added, the candidate needs to be relatable.   "We have historically valued representatives that understand our economy and our struggles," Lessnau said. "We have a very low tolerance for bulls***."

title: Justice Department investigates TV networks, citing possible anti-trust violations
description: President Donald Trump speaks with repor
body:
President Donald Trump speaks with reporters as he arrives on Air Force One, Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026, at Joint Base Andrews, Md.
                
                    Alex Brandon/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Alex Brandon/AP
    

   
   The Justice Department has launched a formal anti-trust investigation into five major U.S. television networks for their actions during a court battle over whether several news outlets should have access to the White House despite angering President Trump.   While the five networks — ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News — did not comment, press rights advocacy groups denounced the move.   "[S]ummoning antitrust authority, on top of the retaliatory actions the White House has already taken to bar certain outlets, is another and even more brazen attempt to try to intimidate journalists," said Bruce Brown, the president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press.   
   Last month, Trump had aides bar CNN, MSNOW and Politico from the White House after blasting them for what he characterized as unfairly negative coverage. The administration stripped White House press passes from more than 70 journalists. The three news organizations sued in federal court to have their access restored. In court, the Justice Department is citing national security grounds for the decision.   The federal judge overseeing the case issued a temporary stay requiring their passes to be restored and says he will make a more enduring decision by Tuesday evening.   However, the White House also blocked CNN from fulfilling its planned shifts as part of the White House television press pool, which includes the other television networks now under investigation. While the news outlets' decision-making is day-to-day, The five have agreed not to substitute for CNN on the days that the administration blocks the network, though they are handling decisions day-to-day.   As part of a longstanding practice, the members of the pool share the logistical burden and the costs of covering Trump's actions in public appearances that take place in smaller places, such as Air Force One. As a result of the ban on CNN, the networks did not cover an event Trump had with Chinese President Xi Jinping.   
   The Justice Department says it is reviewing whether the coordination of that decision constitutes anti-trust behavior, which is to say, anti-competitive.   "Members of the television press pool have proudly boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act," the Justice Department said in a statement Saturday. "The Antitrust Division is investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws."   Four people with direct knowledge of events affirmed the outlines of the investigation. They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly on the matter. The development was first reported by the New York Times.   Michael Dorf, a professor of Constitutional law at Cornell University's law school, says that political motivation on the part of the president or the Justice Department in investigating the networks does not shield them from legal repercussions in court.   But Dorf says it would be subject to a review of whether the networks' actions were reasonable. These were, he says. And he highlights what he calls another "oddity."   "If the networks agreeing not to cover the White House is illegal, why isn't the press pool itself illegal? Presumably the answer is that the kind of cooperation involved in the press pool is necessitated by the limited space in particular venues," Dorf writes in an email. "But if that's a sufficient justification for the cooperation in coverage, why isn't standing up to protect the free press at least as an important a justification?   Part of an ongoing conflict   The incident highlights the increased tensions between the president and the news media. ABC and its parent company Disney are suing Trump's chief broadcast regulator for mandating an immediate review of whether it should hold all eight of its local TV station licenses — threatening a hit to its bottom line. A judge is weighing whether to intervene in the process.   
   Trump has frequently called for ABC (and NBC) to lose their broadcast licenses.   Disney calls the review of the ABC station licenses retaliation over content Trump doesn't like on The View and Jimmy Kimmel Live.   Federal Communications Commission chief Brendan Carr says it's all a question of upholding "the public interest." Under Carr, the FCC has also launched investigations of all other major broadcast networks, including NPR, with the exception of Fox broadcast network, owned by Trump's political ally Rupert Murdoch.   Trump is also suing many major news organizations as an individual. Those outlets include the New York Times, BBC News, and the Wall Street Journal (which is also owned by Murdoch but sometimes draws Trump's ire). ABC and CBS settled earlier lawsuits Trump brought against them.   "The investigation is nonsense," said Seth Stern, Freedom of the Press Foundation's chief of advocacy. "Trump may view the presidency as a business venture, but news outlets' standing up for their constitutional rights has nothing to do with antitrust law."

schema.headline: Justice Department investigates TV networks, citing possible anti-trust violations
